title.narrative: IPAS - Building Commitment and Capacity for Sustainable Abortion Care in DRC
IPAS - Engagemang och kapacitet för säker abortvård i DRK

description.narrative:
Ipas DRC samarbetar med partners för att se till att kvinnor och flickor i Demokratiska republiken Kongo (DRK) kan få tillgång till säker abortvård och utöva sina mänskliga rättigheter till hälsa och autonomi.
Denna insats syftar till att stärka UNFPA: s kapacitet att leverera de resultat som anges i organisationens landprogram för DRK under perioden 2020–2023.
I DRK är alla indikatorer som rör kvinnors sexuella och reproduktiva hälsa och rättigheter (SRHR) oroande, framför allt är den knappa tillgången till preventivmedel och det höga antalet ungdomsgraviditeter alarmerande. Dessutom är den övergripande policymiljön när det gäller SRHR och befolkningsdynamik inte anpassad till landets utmaningar. UNFPA är en nyckelaktör i DRK, vars starka insatser inom ramen för dess globala mandat behövs för att stödja både beslutsfattare, genomförande aktörer på internationell och nationell nivå, och kunna nå ut till olika målgrupper som kvinnor, ungdomar, vårdgivare och institutioner.
Detta institutionella stöd till UNFPA ger dem flexibilitet, frihet och medel för att positionera sig och ge stöd till aktörer inom SRHR och relaterade frågor i landet.

Ipas DRC works with partners to ensure that women and girls in the DRC can access safe abortion care, exercising their human right to health and autonomy. This project aims at providing government stakeholders and selected NGOs, including community organizations and youth-serving, youth-led groups, improved knowledge of the Maputo Protocol and ensuring that they have strengthened capacity and commitment to support women’s rights to broader reproductive health services, including abortion. Key government stakeholders, including the Ministry of Public Health and the Ministry of Gender will the champion national ownership and integration of the Maputo Protocol. This project aligns closely with Sweden’s groundbreaking feminist foreign policy, interest in addressing unsafe abortion’s impact on maternal mortality, and commitment to sustainable health systems that offer equal access to high-quality care.

The project is expected to contribute to expanded access to reproductive health care and rights, including safe abortion, in the DRC. The goal is to strengthen national ownership and the long-term sustainability of reproductive health care, including abortion care in the DRC. The programme goal will be achieved by contributing to an enabling environment through the domestication of the Maputo Protocol and the finalization of standard and guidelines development for safe abortion by the Ministry of Public Health—thus leading to an improvement in comprehensive abortion care access in the country. This process will involve mobilization of stakeholders in the civil society, including youth associations and professional bodies (e.g. midwives association) capable of promoting the rights perspective in the demand and supply sides of vital reproductive health services.

IOM has through this project ensure the strategic management of local public affairs and security issues in the Kalemie territory, IOM supported the development of Local Development Plans (LDP) and Priority Investment Plans (PPI). After an initial phase of data collection and evaluation, the Local Plans and Priority Investment Programs were developed by provincial division of the plan through 55 working sessions and communication with 1,273 participants (including 864 men and 409 women). Following the initial development process, a validation session was organized in the presence of ETD technical departments and stakeholders in Kalemie from 09 to 11 January 2024.
During the fourth year of the project, sustained efforts were made to finalize the process, but the political context did not allow for the final validation of the documents, which remain pending alignment with the provincial government's plan. At the end of the project, these activities were transferred to the Provincial Planning Division, which will ensure the continuation of the validation process and the implementation of the plans developed. IOM continued to support the inclusive and participatory local governance mechanisms, that have been established during previous reporting periods, with strengthened capacities in mediation, identification of security challenges, and promotion of dialogue and social cohesion. Efforts focused on consolidating the achievements of previous years by monitoring and strengthening existing mechanisms. Refresher training courses were organized on the roles and responsibilities of Local Committees in villages in order to maintain their level of commitment and performance. In addition, specific support was provided to Local Peace and Development Structures (SLPD) to preserve and revitalize existing EWS in place. This approach has helped to sustain community mechanisms, ensure the continuity of local initiatives, and consolidate social cohesion within beneficiary communities. It also ensuring full involvement and transparent decision making of all community members at local level. This has strengthened local ownership of project activities.
Maternal and child health services, including referral mechanisms and psychosocial support for victims, have also enhanced the mental wellbeing of the most vulnerable members of the community and contributed to collaborative efforts for peaceful coexistence. In accordance with the project exit strategy, a process of transferring skills to state technical services was carried out to ensure ownership and sustainability of the achievements. With this in mind, the Local Peace and Development Committees (CLPD)[1] were brought into line with the provisions of Provincial Decree No. 094/CAB/GOUVTANG/2023 of 10 October 2023, on the creation, organization, and functioning of local development committees. This alignment ensured the institutional compliance of the community structures supported by the project and promoted their official recognition by the provincial authorities.
To ensure the strategic management of local public affairs and security issues in the Kalemie territory, IOM supported the development of Local Development Plans (LDP) and Priority Investment Plans (PPI). After an initial phase of data collection and evaluation, the Local Plans and Priority Investment Programs were developed by provincial division of the plan through 55 working sessions and communication with 1,273 participants (including 864 men and 409 women). Following the initial development process, a validation session was organized in the presence of ETD technical departments and stakeholders in Kalemie from 09 to 11 January 2024.
A transfer and accountability agreement were signed between the Groupement Moni, Tumbwe Chiefdom, and the Provincial Decentralization Division, in the presence of IOM. This formal act constitutes a key institutional achievement, marking the continuity of the SLPDs' work after the end of the project and their gradual integration into the local governance system. The direct effects observed reflect a concrete impact on governance and community stability: provincial authorities now recognize SLPDs as legitimate intermediaries in the implementation of local peace and development actions. Decentralization experts have praised the relevance of these structures and have committed to providing followup and technical support, thereby ensuring the sustainability of the project's achievements and the consolidation of stability in decentralized territorial entities.
Furthermore, during the reporting period, 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025, the following key achievements were reached: Over 260 households were issued official land tenure documents, thereby ensuring the longterm provision of adequate shelter through land rights for returnee households and vulnerable community households. Improved social cohesion and mental wellbeing of host and returnee communities through inclusive and participatory governance mechanisms, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). These mechanisms have enabled better integration of communities in the management of local affairs and promoted peaceful coexistence through increased awareness raising communities affected by displacement. Psychosocial support was a key element, with the establishment of specialized focal points and the provision of 4,584 MHPSS services, thus strengthening the fragmented social fabric. In addition, the introduction of complaints management committees and early warning systems (EWS) in the five priority communities have helped to promote the peaceful resolution of disputes. These initiatives have reduced ethnic tensions and helped restore a climate of peace in communities. Strengthening the economic resilience of host and returnee communities through the creation of economic opportunities[2] for over 642 heads of households, including 440 women and 202 men. This has considerably improved access to financial resources and enabled the development of Income Generating Activities (IGA), thus contributing to the economic autonomy of returnee and host communities. Improved and strengthened access to basic services for over 12,000 people through the rehabilitation of nine priority community infrastructures in the targeted villages which facilitated access to essential services such as water, education and health. The experiences, lessons learned, and best practices from this project served as the basis for improving the content of the provincial strategy on sustainable solutions, which was approved by the provincial government in December 2024. The construction of an elementary school in Saliboko has provided an education and learning environment that meets standards and has given access and improved study conditions to 721 pupils ex IDPs as well as host communities, including 392 girls (we vistied this school and saw it fully functional with nutritious food provided with WFP, a school garden being developed by FAO to enhance nutrition as well as educational materials from UNICEF) . On the initiative of the community, and in response to the need, the elementary school buildings are now also being used to run a secondary school (during afternoon hours) for 161 pupils, including an additional 51 girls. Construction of 7 water point, which have improved access to drinking water, reducing the risk of waterborne diseases and improving the overall health of communities. They have also strengthened community resilience, promoted hygiene and fostered social cohesion, as many conflicts were linked to water shortages.The rehabilitation and construction of the 2 bridges and scuppers have facilitated community access and exchanges with the city for the sale of agricultural produce. These structures have also improved community safety by facilitating access to the various patrols, while enhancing fluidity, mobility and community development. They have also reduced transport costs, while facilitating the sale of agricultural produce and access to local markets 2 health facilities have brought people closer to healthcare services, while offering them quality care. They have also strengthened community access to primary health care. As an annex to a health center, these health posts provide care to the population of the health area concerned, through the integrated implementation of the minimum package of activities of health projects and programs at village/neighborhood level. Construction of 2 vocational training centers, have helped to reduce the impact of unemployment, delinquency and poverty, and to encourage the population to take economic responsibility for themselves. For the first time in the area, communities have access to fully equipped facilities, with classrooms and workshops offering a range of vocational training options, including cutting and sewing, carpentry, masonry, motorcycle mechanics, pastry-making, soapmaking and beauty and hairdressing.
Based on the capacity building support provided during the first three years of the project, this reporting period saw the implementation of different activities to promote mental health and provide community psychosocial support. Overall services provided for 4,584 beneficiaries, including 2,647 women and 1,937 men. The services offered as part of the psychosocial support activities were: 18 individual and group counseling sessions for 113 beneficiaries. 108 emotional support sessions for around 35 persons (23 women and 12 men) 376 group discussion sessions.
23 small scale community conflict mediation sessions. 344 psychoeducation sessions on stress management for around 121 persons ( 47 men and 74 women) Case management and home visits to 9 people with major depressive disorders, suicidal thoughts and attempts. participants in recreational games (sixaside, a checkers, awalé, skipping, train). These activities helped to improve the psychosocial wellbeing of the beneficiaries by alleviating their psychosocial distress, improving their day today functioning and helping them to implement effective coping strategies and social cohesion. The psychotherapy provided also helped to bring about significant changes in beneficiaries' cognitive, emotional and behavioral functioning.
